image_description:
1. **Chart type**: Word cloud (tag cloud).

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses a **single-panel free-form layout**.  
   - No faceting, stacking, axes, or small multiples.  
   - Words are arranged spatially to fill the canvas, with **font size** indicating magnitude.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Search term / word (e.g., “gas,” “milk,” “meat”) | Categorical/nominal | Text label (word content), spatial placement |
| Frequency / count (shown by word size and small adjacent numbers) | Quantitative | Font size of word; numeric label next to each word |
| Color grouping (orange vs. dark gray words) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of text |

Notes:
- No explicit temporal or ordinal variable is visible.
- Position appears used for layout rather than encoding a measured variable.

comments.raw_comment: The first thing that I noticed when looking at this graph was that the biggest word was gas, mentioned a total of 904 times. I figure that out of all of the words that were depicted in this visual, that is the one that may have had the most universal impact on the people surveyed. Gas is necessary to commute anywhere with a motor vehicle, whereas some other words that were mentioned in the visual do not have the same level of necessity and lack of substitutes. I noticed that food items were colored orange and that they made up the majority of the goods mentioned, with milk, meat, and beef as the top three foods. I wonder how this survey was conducted, like what groups of people they decided to survey. I wonder how the survey and the most mentioned words would look depending on different socioeconomic groups. I wonder what the visual would look like if it was organized based on the actual impact that inflation had on the price of the good. I imagine that although some of the products mentioned might not have had the highest overall price change due to inflation but rather the most used products make it so people are more likely to notice.

There is such a large demand for the basic necessities but a supply shortage for all of these products. Milk, meat, beef, chicken, and eggs are all greatly consumed products in the world and so there is a huge demand for these foods because we live in a time where no one knows what will happen next. Recently, specifically within the last month, gas prices have grown higher than ever. This is because of the war between Ukraine and Russia. I wonder how long it is going to take for the gas prices to go down after the war ends. I also wonder if the crisis in Ukraine is going to affect products like milk, meat, etc., harsher in the next few weeks. This affects me and my community because I see these prices every day and I have to pay for these prices. A catchy headline is "Product Prices Increasing, Supply of Products Decreasing!"

1. The graph is a list of products that people surveyed said have increased in price. Food items are orange, and other items are black. Next to each item is the number of people that mentioned the item. Gas has the highest count by far at 904 responses. Every item listed has at least 7 responses.

2. I wonder why there is such a large gap between the top two responses, gas has 904 but milk has 455. I wonder why cars and used cars are listed separately. I wonder why some products were classified as food or not food. For example dog food, pet food, and oil are not counted as food products, but shampoo is counted as food. I’m surprised that only 22 people responded “everything” since because of inflation that’s very true.

3.  Inflation affects everyone. In the US minimum wage has not been increasing appropriately with inflation, so increasing prices impact everyone.

4. “What has gotten the most expensive?”

Welcome to Wednesday's live moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graph shows the Feb. 2022 responses to the survey question:  Name specific products and services whose higher prices have stood out to them over the past year.  

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?”, “What do you wonder?"  and “How will this affect you and your community?”  Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in this graph. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included this graph and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, April 1 with moderation on Wednesday, April 6.  The topic – biodiversity.  Keep noticing and wondering.
